summary.text: 天 (tiān) is the character for “sky” or “heaven.” Its early forms are analyzed either as a person with the head marked, perhaps associated with head or top, or as a depiction of heaven; surviving evidence does not settle the character’s earliest meaning.

formation.text: Pictographic, in the interpretation that the graph depicts a human figure with an emphasized head. In that analysis, 大 represents the standing person and the upper mark represents the head; paleographers describe that mark as later simplified to a horizontal stroke. A competing account takes the word’s original meaning to be “sky” and treats the older graph as an anthropomorphic depiction of heaven. The dossier supports no phonetic component.

components.text: 大 is the human figure in the head-marked analysis of early 天. In this graph it depicts a person; it is not identified as a sound component.
一 represents the emphasized head in the paleographic analysis; its mark is described as later reduced to a horizontal stroke. The graph’s shape is not evidence that 一 supplies sound.

history.text: The curated Shang-style oracle-script illustration is a modern redraw of an identified exemplar, not an inspected artifact. Its human figure and marked head illustrate one paleographic interpretation; it does not establish the original meaning or a sequence of semantic changes.

Paleographic accounts describe the head mark as simplified into a horizontal stroke. This is a reported graphic change, not evidence of corruption. The Eastern Han Shuowen entry analyzes the graph as 一 plus 大 and glosses 天 through 顛, “top of the head”; that is a historical dictionary interpretation, not proof of the earliest spoken meaning.

Shang examples are reported for head-related use and for 天邑商 alongside 大邑商. The latter comparison supports interchange or close relation between 天 and 大 in some early expressions, but does not establish that the spoken word 天 began with the meaning “great.” Later reported examples include bronze 天命 and 天子 and Warring States 天命 and 天下; the dossier does not establish an unbroken semantic path among these uses.

The head-first analysis competes with an account that takes “sky” as the original word meaning and the human-like old graph as an anthropomorphic representation of heaven. The available evidence does not decide between these accounts or provide absolute dates for the cited individual inscriptions.

uncertainties.text: Early head-related uses, the 天/大 interchange, and the competing sky-first interpretation do not establish a single earliest spoken sense or a complete development from head or top to sky and heaven.

The dossier reports competing Old Chinese reconstructions in distinct systems and early dialectal variation, but offers no component sound relation to explain: neither 一 nor 大 is supported as phonetic in 天.

senses.text: Sky/heaven is the common meaning reported for 天, and an account in the dossier proposes it as the original word meaning. Early inscription evidence and analyses remain contested, so this designation records the earliest-attested sense category available here, not a proven original meaning or priority over head-related use.

senses.period: Shang oracle-bone corpus; individual token dates unresolved
senses.text: A head-related use is reported for an oracle-bone context. The paleographic interpretation connects it with the head-marked human figure, while the exact relationship between this use and the word for sky/heaven remains unsettled.

senses.gloss: “great” or use in a name expression
senses.period: Shang-Zhou material; individual token dates unresolved
senses.text: A specialist discussion cites 天邑商 alongside 大邑商 and reports an older gloss of 天 as “great” in one phrase. These examples show early interchange or close relation in usage, not that “great” was the word’s original meaning.

senses.gloss: divine or sovereign uses, including “Heaven” in compounds
senses.period: Bronze inscriptions and later Warring States texts; individual token dates unresolved
senses.text: Reported bronze and bamboo-slip examples include 天帝, 天命, 天子, and 天下. These compound contexts attest divine, sovereign, or “under heaven” uses, but their word-level meanings do not by themselves establish separate single-character senses or a dated chain of change.

developments.text: A paleographic account proposes extension from the head or head-top association to the sky above. A competing account treats “sky” as original; the evidence does not establish which chronology is correct.

limitations.text: The dossier does not supply absolute dates for each cited inscription, establish one certain earliest spoken sense, or demonstrate a complete semantic sequence. The early graph’s attestation and the spoken word’s earliest meaning remain distinct questions.

overview.text: 天 means “sky” or “heaven.” One leading graphic analysis sees a standing person with the head marked; another takes the word “sky” as original. The early evidence does not settle which meaning came first.

components.text: The large lower shape depicts a standing person in the human-figure analysis of the old graph.
The upper mark is interpreted as the emphasized head; paleographers say it was later simplified into a horizontal stroke.

relationships.text: In the head-marked human-figure analysis, 大 depicts the standing person in the early graph.
Paleographic analyses interpret the upper mark as the person’s emphasized head; they report that it was later simplified to a horizontal stroke.
